title: Teller County well depths and drilling costs
meta_description: In Teller County, the median well depth is about 260 ft and the median yield is 6 gpm. Here’s what that means for drilling and buying land.
h1: Understanding water wells in Teller County, Colorado
intro_html:
Teller County wells are classic mountain bedrock wells: variable depth, decent but not guaranteed production, and drilling into fractured rock instead of a clean sand aquifer. The state has records on 10,770 permits here, with 7,315 reporting total depth and 4,334 reporting pump yield, so we have a solid picture of what you’re likely to hit.

If you’re buying land or planning a new house around Woodland Park, Divide, Florissant, or the Cripple Creek–Victor side, the numbers below are the best guide for setting a realistic drilling budget and judging an existing well.

sections.heading: How deep Teller County wells usually go
sections.html:
Across Teller County, the median well depth is 260 feet. The middle half run from about 150 to 400 feet, and roughly 40% of wells are in the 300–600 foot range. Another 7% go past 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 3,535 feet, which shows how stubborn fractured rock can be in spots.

About 12% of wells are under 100 feet, but you shouldn’t plan on that. For bids, a driller is going to look at nearby wells and probably budget you closer to that 260–400 foot band. This is all hard mountain rock — mostly fractured granite and other crystalline bedrock — so footage, not loose overburden, is what drives the cost here.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water homes actually get here
sections.html:
On production, Teller County is reasonably solid for household wells but not a slam dunk. The median reported yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between about 2.0 and 9.3 gpm. That’s fine for a single home on an exempt domestic permit, assuming decent storage and plumbing.

The risk shows up in the low end: about 11% of wells report under 1 gpm, and another 32% are between 1 and 5 gpm. Those can still support a house, but you’re relying more on storage tanks and careful use. Around 53% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, with only 5% higher than that, so “gusher” wells are the exception in this fractured-bedrock setting.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the table
sections.html:
Static water levels in Teller County are typically well below the surface but not extreme for mountain terrain. The median depth to water is about 95 feet, and the middle half of measurements fall between roughly 60 and 140 feet below ground. That’s the standing water level, not total well depth.

Looking over time, median water levels were about 114 feet in the 1960s, then shallower in the 1970s (76 feet) and 1980s (52 feet). More recent readings show deeper levels again: about 85 feet in the 2010s and 105 feet in the 2020s. That points to some rebound followed by a modest deepening, not a straight-line crash, but it’s still a reason to pay attention to current water levels on any older well you’re buying.

sections.heading: Who drills here and how active permits are
sections.html:
Drilling in Teller County is dominated by a few outfits that know the local fractured rock. Mountain Well Improvement LLC (Wiley, David D.) shows up on 1,774 wells, and Woods Drilling Inc. under William D. Woods and William L. Woods appears on another 2,762 wells combined. That much history means your driller can usually reference nearby completions and depths.

Permitting ramped up in the 1970s and 1980s, with 1,514 and 1,799 permits in those decades, then peaked in the 1990s at 2,581. Activity stayed strong in the 2000s with 1,791 permits, then tapered to 814 in the 2010s and 688 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2025, so new wells are still going in across Woodland Park, Divide, and the Cripple Creek–Victor area.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Teller County
sections.html:
Here you’re almost always drilling into hard fractured granite or similar bedrock, at a typical rate of about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 260-foot median depth, that puts the bare drilled hole around $16,900 to $26,000 just for drilling and casing.

Once you add a pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a finished median-depth well usually ends up in the ballpark of $22,900 to $38,000. If your neighbors are all in that 300–600 foot band, assume the high side of those ranges when you budget. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells here, so you’re not buying into a known sandstone aquifer with predictable target depths; it’s all fractured-bedrock variability.

sections.heading: Risks: low yield, mining legacy, and siting issues
sections.html:
Most wells here are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a smaller number tagged as Fractured Granite or Fractured Crystalline. That geology gives you workable household wells but also explains the 11% of wells under 1 gpm and the 7% that had to go past 600 feet. Low yield and deeper-than-expected drilling are the main water risks.

Teller County also has a mining legacy: about 276 historic mine features and 12 mapped EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles, plus 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. That doesn’t make your water unsafe by default, but it does mean water-quality testing is smart, especially closer to Cripple Creek, Victor, and older workings. On small lots, you also have to fit septic far enough from the well and avoid old mine waste when you lay out the house and leach field.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well in Teller County
sections.html:
Most permitted wells here are for domestic or household use (about 91%), with small shares for stock, irrigation, and monitoring. That’s good news if you’re putting a single home on 35 acres or more, since the typical well and yield profile was built around that use. But you still need to check a specific property’s details, not just county averages.

For an existing well, pull the DWR permit, confirm total depth, yield test results, and static level, and then order a recent water-quality test, especially in areas with historic mining or mapped PFAS sites. For raw land, study nearby well logs around Woodland Park, Divide, Florissant, Cripple Creek, Victor, and Midland to see real depths and yields, then budget based on the deeper neighbors. Finally, make sure your driveway, septic, and building envelope can all be laid out without crowding the well.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Teller County, Colorado?
faq.a: State records for Teller County show a median well depth of about 260 feet. The middle half of wells fall between roughly 150 and 400 feet, with about 40% in the 300–600 foot range and 7% deeper than 600 feet. Around 12% are under 100 feet, but planning on a 260–400 foot well is more realistic for new drilling.

faq.q: How much water do Teller County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields in Teller County have a median of 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between about 2.0 and 9.3 gpm. Roughly 11% of wells report under 1 gpm and 32% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. About 53% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and only 5% exceed 15 gpm, so moderate domestic supplies are typical.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Teller County, CO?
faq.a: In Teller County’s fractured granite and gneiss, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the 260-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $16,900–$26,000. By the time you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished median-depth well usually ends up roughly $22,900–$38,000, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Teller County?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location. Teller County has about 276 historic mine features, 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within roughly 10 miles. Many homes use wells safely, but you should always do a lab test for bacteria, metals, and other contaminants on your specific well, especially near mining areas.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Teller County?
faq.a: Static water level data are limited but give some clues. Median depth to water was about 114 feet in the 1960s, then shallower in the 1970s and 1980s (down to 52 feet), before rising again to about 85 feet in the 2010s and 105 feet in the 2020s. That suggests some deepening in recent decades but not a simple, continuous decline over the whole record.
